but conjunction

classical

Catull. 61.90: sed morāris, abit diēs

Traupman 285

sed

conjunction, first in its clause · Wiktionary

The plain “but”, which sets the second thing against the first; after a negative, “not … but” is nōn … sed. Many English “buts” need no word in Latin, where two clauses side by side make the contrast; and a light “but” that only moves on is autem (see however). Don’t open sentence after sentence with sed.

Other words

  • at — but (sharply); but, you say

    conjunction, first in its clause · also used · classical · Cic. Sen. 21: at memoria minuitur; Verg. G. 4.6: in tenuī labor; at tenuis nōn glōria; Traupman 285 · Wiktionary

    A sharper “but”: an objection in speech (“but, you’ll say …”), a protest (At!), or a sudden turn to another person or scene.

  • vērum — but (rather)

    conjunction, first in its clause · also used · classical · Phaedr. 3 prol. 49–50: neque enim notāre singulōs mēns est mihi, vērum ipsam vītam et mōrēs hominum ostendere; Traupman 285 · Wiktionary

    After a negative, the same as sed; in nōn modo … vērum etiam, not only … but also.

Examples

  • sed morāris, abit diēs

    but you are dawdling, and the day is goingCatull. 61.90

  • curre, sed īnstrūctus

    run, but go equippedMart. 4.10.5

  • nōn est mī male, sed bene ac beātē

    I’m not badly off, but well and happyCatull. 14.10

  • at memoria minuitur. crēdō, nisi eam exerceās

    but memory fades. — I dare say, if you don’t exercise itCic. Sen. 21

  • in tenuī labor; at tenuis nōn glōria

    the work is on a small thing, but the glory is not smallVerg. G. 4.6

See also however, not only … but also, whereas.
